title: Who Sets the Pace of Judge Hacking?Judge Capability versus the Policy–Judge Gap

paper.title: Who Sets the Pace of Judge Hacking? Judge Capability versus the Policy–Judge Gap
paper.abstract: Abstract When a policy is trained with GRPO against a frozen, reference-free LLM judge, the judge accepts more of its answers, but in a post-hoc analysis of saved logs we detect no gain in held-out greedy accuracy: in all 12 (policy, judge) cells, the seed-mean greedy accuracy on held-out GSM8K problems never rose more than 0.04 0.04 above step 0 (single seeds: at most + 0.085 +0.085 ). A gold-reward control with the same recipe (2 seeds, 150 steps, 500 problems) raised the 1.5B policy’s greedy accuracy by + 0.054 +0.054 [ 0.013 , 0.096 ] [0.013,0.096] , so for this policy the flat accuracy is specific to the judge reward; for the 0.5B policy, gold reward also gave no detectable gain ( + 0.022 +0.022 [ − 0.015 , 0.059 ] [-0.015,0.059] ). In the four rising cells we checked at step 50, including the largest rise, the rise in training-rollout accuracy is mostly sampling sharpening: held-out temperature-1 accuracy rose, but greedy accuracy did not detectably change. The gold-reward cells are also sharpening at step 50, so this early rise is a property of the short recipe, not a sign of judge exploitation. We therefore ask whether the policy–judge gap or the judge sets how far and how fast RL exploits the judge’s false positives. We train 0.5B and 1.5B Qwen2.5 policies against four judges at least as large (Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B/7B, Llama-3.2-3B; 26 runs), and the 1.5B policy against one smaller judge (Qwen3-0.6B; 4 runs). The depth of judge hacking (the plateau) tracks the judge: it correlates with judge AUC (Spearman − 0.69 -0.69 [ − 0.94 , − 0.14 ] [-0.94,-0.14] over 12 cells), and within a family the larger judge is fooled less deeply. For the pace (onset), the two pre-specified pairs contradict the gap account (the cell with the larger gap was fooled 2.6 × 2.6\times sooner at a fooled fraction of 0.3 0.3 , a version added post hoc; 3.5 × 3.5\times at the pre-specified 0.5 0.5 ), but with 12 cells we cannot formally separate judge AUC from the gap for either endpoint (difference in correlations: plateau − 0.38 -0.38 [ − 0.95 , 0.00 ] [-0.95,0.00] ; onset 0.36 0.36 [ 0.00 , 0.91 ] [0.00,0.91] ). The smaller judge was not fooled sooner than a judge as large as the policy, but it also differs in family and chat template. The pre-registered primary rule found a policy effect only under the 7B judge; at threshold 0.3 0.3 that effect is gone, and a pre-registered secondary contrast shows one under the 3B judge instead (the larger policy is fooled later). In a blind test on three held-out judges, a hash-locked step-0 predictor did not beat step-0 AUC, but three cells cannot separate them. At 7–8B, judges from three families plateaued at 0.37 0.37 , 0.67 0.67 and 0.85 0.85 .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: LLM judges and model-based verifiers are used as RL rewards where no hand-written verifier exists ( Ma et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . A judge that sees a candidate answer scores plausibility, not correctness, and RL can raise its acceptance rate while true accuracy stays flat ( Zhou, 2026 , “more convincing, not more correct”, in a reasoning-suppressed regime;) . Our logs show this pattern (Section 3 ). So we do not measure overoptimization in the sense of Gao et al. (2023) , where the proxy first helps and then hurts. We measure how fast and how far GRPO exploits a false-positive region that the judge has from step 0. What sets this pace? In the gap account , the capability gap between judge and policy sets it: judge hacking “worsens precisely when the judge is weaker than the policy” ( Kenton et al., 2026 ) , and a model of oversight as a function of the capability gap points the same way ( Engels et al., 2025 ) . In the judge account , the judge itself sets it. Only a crossed design, with cells of similar gap and different judges, separates the two. In the main design the judges are 1–16 × \times larger than the policy and both policies are weak solvers, so there we test the gap account only where the judge is at least as strong as the policy. One added cell pairs the 1.5B policy with a smaller judge (Qwen3-0.6B). This judge solves GSM8K about as well as the policy and comes from another family, so the cell is not a clean test of a judge weaker than the policy. We run GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) on GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) . Every stage had a hashed specification before its runs, and we report all deviations (Appendix A ). Our findings: (1) judge-RL did not detectably improve held-out greedy accuracy (post hoc): no cell of 12 showed a seed-mean gain above 0.04 0.04 , judge acceptance rose in all 11 cells where we logged it, and in the four rising cells we checked, including the largest rise, the rise in training-rollout accuracy is mostly sampling sharpening; a gold-reward control with the same recipe gained + 0.054 +0.054 [ 0.013 , 0.096 ] [0.013,0.096] for P1.5, so there the flat accuracy is specific to the judge reward, but only + 0.022 +0.022 [ − 0.015 , 0.059 ] [-0.015,0.059] for P0.5, so there it is not (Section 3 ); (2) in our cells with judge ≥ \geq policy, the depth of judge hacking (the plateau) tracks the judge : it correlates with judge AUC (Spearman − 0.69 -0.69 [ − 0.94 , − 0.14 ] [-0.94,-0.14] over 12 cells), and within a family the larger judge is fooled less deeply; for the pace (onset), the two pre-specified pairs contradict the gap account at two onset thresholds (descriptive contrasts), but with 12 cells we cannot formally separate judge AUC from the gap for either endpoint (difference in correlations: plateau − 0.38 -0.38 [ − 0.95 , 0.00 ] [-0.95,0.00] ; onset 0.36 0.36 [ 0.00 , 0.91 ] [0.00,0.91] ); the one cell with a smaller judge shows no evidence of a gap effect, but its control plateau is near the ceiling and family and template are confounded (Section 4 ); (3) a blind test of step-0 predictors is inconclusive and does not favor the screened predictor over AUC (Section 5 ); (4) same-size judges from different families differ widely (Section 5.1 ).

3 Judge-RL did not detectably raise held-out greedy accuracy
sections.text: No cell’s seed mean gained more than about one binomial standard error ( 0.033 0.033 – 0.035 0.035 at n = 200 n=200 ): the largest seed-mean gain over step 0 was + 0.037 +0.037 (P1.5 × \times Q1.5, step 40), and each maximum is taken over 20–25 evaluation steps (Figure 2 ; Table 3 ). Single seeds reached up to + 0.085 +0.085 (P1.5 × \times Q3), and we ran no equivalence test, so small gains are not excluded. Under Q7 accuracy stayed flat; under weaker judges it fell, for P0.5 to 0.09 0.09 (Q1.5) and 0.02 0.02 (O1) by step 150. Judge acceptance of the same held-out answers rose in every cell where we logged it (all but stage 6), for example from 0.57 0.57 to 0.91 0.91 under Q3. Training-rollout accuracy did rise in 11 of 12 cells (P0.5: from about 0.22 0.22 to 0.29 0.29 – 0.47 0.47 ; Figure 3 ). But training-rollout accuracy in steps 1–10 is far below greedy accuracy ( 0.22 0.22 vs. 0.33 0.33 ; training problems at temperature 1 vs. held-out problems, greedy), and the peaks land near the greedy level. A sharper sampling distribution would produce the same rise, and a pre-registered check (stage 6) classifies both main cells as sharpening. On the 200 held-out problems, the step-50 checkpoints of P0.5 × \times Q3 and P1.5 × \times Q3 gained + 0.13 +0.13 [ 0.09 , 0.17 ] [0.09,0.17] and + 0.23 +0.23 [ 0.19 , 0.27 ] [0.19,0.27] in temperature-1 accuracy over the SFT policy, close to the rise of the training rollouts ( + 0.14 +0.14 and + 0.23 +0.23 ). Greedy accuracy, measured in the same pass, changed by only + 0.004 +0.004 [ − 0.054 , 0.062 ] [-0.054,0.062] and + 0.035 +0.035 [ − 0.024 , 0.094 ] [-0.024,0.094] (Table 7 ). So in these cells the rise in rollout accuracy is the policy’s temperature-1 samples concentrating on its greedy answers, with no detectable change in greedy accuracy (upper bounds + 0.06 +0.06 and + 0.09 +0.09 ). In the four rising cells we checked at step 50, including the largest rise (P0.5 × \times Q7: + 0.147 +0.147 [ 0.113 , 0.181 ] [0.113,0.181] at temperature 1, + 0.026 +0.026 [ − 0.023 , 0.075 ] [-0.023,0.075] greedy; also P0.5 × \times O7), the rise is mostly sharpening. The check covers step 50 only; the P0.5 × \times Q7 rollout peak is near step 130. Appendix C gives the details, including a failed validity check that does not change the classification. Gold-reward control (stage 7). We repeated the recipe with the gold label as reward (1 if the lenient label is correct, else 0), 2 seeds and 150 steps per policy, and measured the step-150 checkpoints on 500 held-out problems (Table 7 ). sections.heading: 6 Related work and positioning
sections.text: The closest work is Zhou (2026) : Qwen3 policies on GSM8K trained by self-play against reference-free judgments raise the judge’s pass rate while accuracy stays flat, and the errors transfer across judge families. We see the same with separate frozen judges and add a crossed design. On transfer, hacks found against Q3 and Q7 partly fool Llama-3.2-3B ( h L h_{L} 0.07–0.36), but hacks found against Q1.5 hardly do ( h L h_{L} 0.05 0.05 and − 0.18 -0.18 ). The error types do not point to hacks that exploit a weak judge’s arithmetic slips: such slips are not more common under weaker judges (Q1.5 10/40, Q3 12/40, Q7 9/40; Table 8 ). Kenton et al. (2026) study a judge weaker than the policy; our one cell with a smaller judge solves about as well as the policy and comes from another family, so it is not a clean test of that regime. Huang et al. (2026) find that more accurate model-based math verifiers are still hacked in RL, especially after fine-tuning, so our AUC result applies only to zero-shot instruct judges. A static math reward benchmark tracks best-of- n n policy outcomes ( Kim et al., 2024 ) , and Zhang (2026) run a pre-registered GRPO study on code in which a pre-training audit tracks rewarded false positives; we differ in using LLM judges, judge-side step-0 metrics and a hash-locked selection before a blind test. More capable agents can exploit misspecified rewards more, with phase transitions ( Pan et al., 2022 ) ; two policy sizes cannot exclude such a threshold. Raychev et al. (2025) varied policy and generative reward-model size (Qwen3 0.6B–14B, creative writing, online DPO) and found reward-model scale most decisive, even when the reward model far exceeds the policy; the submission was not accepted at ICLR 2026. Overoptimization and predicting RL outcomes. Gao et al. (2023) showed that the coefficients of the overoptimization curve of a learned proxy reward model change smoothly with reward-model size, and that a 6B policy overoptimizes about as much as a 1.2B policy (two policy sizes; they note that this contradicts other internal findings). Our policy-size contrasts are mixed (an effect under Q7 at h ≥ 0.5 h\geq 0.5 and under Q3 at h ≥ 0.3 h\geq 0.3 , Section 4 ); we differ in the judge (a prompted, frozen LLM without a reference), the endpoint (false positives on wrong answers), the design (equal-gap cells), and the outcome (no gold improvement). Static benchmarks such as RewardBench ( Lambert et al., 2025 ) are standard; several works ask whether such metrics predict RL outcomes ( Frick et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Wen et al., 2025b ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Razin et al., 2025 ) . Our blind test is a small pre-registered instance for frozen LLM judges. Hacking LLM judges and oversight. LLM judges have known biases ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) and can be fooled by short strings ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) . AdvJudge-Zero ( Li et al., 2025 ) finds short control tokens that flip judge verdicts and shows that a hardened judge removes false-positive spikes under GRPO on MATH and GSM8K; its hacks are token-level, while ours are fluent, confident solutions with a wrong setup or an arithmetic slip (Appendix C ). RL can make answers more convincing without making them more correct ( Wen et al., 2025a ; Zhou, 2026 ) . Liu et al. (2026) find that non-reasoning judges are hacked easily in non-verifiable post-training, while reasoning judges lead to policies that do well under a gold judge partly through adversarial outputs. Kenton et al. (2026) train against a frozen judge weaker than the policy and find that weakening the judge further speeds up hacking, which agrees in direction with our within-family trend. A gap-based model of oversight ( Engels et al., 2025 ) motivates the gap account; weak-to-strong work studies what a weaker supervisor can elicit from a stronger model ( Burns et al., 2024 ) . Other related work. Scalable-oversight protocols ( Bowman et al., 2022 ; Khan et al., 2024 ; Kenton et al., 2024 ) study how a weaker supervisor can oversee a stronger model, and Engels et al. (2025) model oversight success as a function of the capability gap in task-specific Elo. Building on the setup of Gao et al. (2023) , reward-model ensembles were proposed as a mitigation ( Coste et al., 2024 ) , and later work studied overoptimization in direct alignment methods ( Rafailov et al., 2024 ) . LLMs can also be trained as verifiers or reward models ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ; Lightman et al., 2024 ) , including generative verifiers ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Our judges are untrained instruct models used zero-shot; training them, or letting them commit to their own answer first ( Zhou, 2026 ) , are defenses we do not test.

sections.heading: 7 Limitations and conclusion
sections.text: Limitations. (i) One task, prompt and recipe; no KL penalty; single-token judges without chain of thought; policies ≤ 1.5 {\leq}1.5 B, judges ≤ 8 {\leq}8 B. Only one judge is smaller than the policy (0.6B vs. 1.5B); it solves about as well ( 0.585 0.585 vs. 0.61 0.61 ) and comes from another family and template, so a judge weaker than the policy is tested only in one confounded cell. (ii) 2–4 seeds per cell; the predictor test has 3 held-out cells and one policy. (iii) Screening candidates, the plateau endpoint, the test’s pass rule and the step coordinate were set after some outcomes were known (Appendix A ). (iv) Gold labels are parsers (5.7% errors in the per-answer check, done by an LLM agent and by the author). (v) The gold-reward control has 2 seeds, 150 steps and one learning rate; the 12-cell correlation intervals treat cells as independent. Conclusion. In our 12 cells of GRPO against frozen, reference-free LLM judges, judge-RL did not detectably improve held-out greedy accuracy. A gold-reward control with the same recipe did improve it for P1.5, so there the flat accuracy is specific to the judge reward; for P0.5 it did not, so there it is not. In the four rising cells we checked, the early rise in training-rollout accuracy was mostly sampling sharpening, as it was under gold reward. Where the judge was at least as large as the policy, the depth of judge hacking (the plateau) tracks the judge: it correlates with judge AUC (Spearman − 0.69 -0.69 [ − 0.94 , − 0.14 ] [-0.94,-0.14] over 12 cells), and within a family the larger judge is fooled less deeply. For the pace (onset), the two pre-specified pairs contradict the gap account, but with 12 cells we cannot formally separate judge AUC from the gap for either endpoint (difference in correlations: plateau − 0.38 -0.38 [ − 0.95 , 0.00 ] [-0.95,0.00] ; onset 0.36 0.36 [ 0.00 , 0.91 ] [0.00,0.91] ); this rests on descriptive pairs and 2–4 seeds per cell. One cell with a smaller judge gave no evidence of a gap effect, but its control plateau was near the ceiling and it is confounded with judge family.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: This study has no human subjects and uses no personal data: all answers were generated by open-weight models on GSM8K problems. The licenses of all models and data are listed in Appendix B . Our results show that zero-shot LLM judges for math are easy to exploit with RL, and we report this as a caution for those who use such judges as rewards. The hacks we observed are ordinary wrong solutions, and we introduce no new attack method.

sections.heading: Appendix E Toward a predictive account
sections.text: The pre-registered test leaves step-0 AUC as the best simple predictor within one policy and shows that the logit scale does not transfer across families. A stronger version needs (i) both policies on the held-out judges, so that the pooled-row advantage seen in screening can be tested; (ii) at least three sizes in two or more new families; (iii) predictors that are invariant to the judge’s logit scale; (iv) a judge smaller than the policy from the policy’s own family, to separate size from family and template; and (v) a second task (a MATH subset). With the 0.5B policy, one task, 4 seeds and 200 steps, a new cell cost 2.5–4.4 A100-hours in stage 5.
